bearer.description: The token from get_token, on every API request after login.

client_basic.description: OAuth2 client authentication for the token endpoint only. The client id and secret are fixed published constants, the same in openHAB's binding and the planbnet/livisi library: "clientId" / "clientPass", i.e. the header "Authorization: Basic Y2xpZW50SWQ6Y2xpZW50UGFzcw==". They identify no user and no unit.

cloud.failure_mode: Retired on 2024-03-01: no accounts, app login, remote access, push notifications, cloud backup, voice assistants or IFTTT, and LIVISI said the stored data was deleted. Controllers keep running locally (Local SmartHome, automatically enabled by the Jan/Feb 2024 updates), with rules executing on the controller.
cloud.notes: Timeline: heise reported on 2022-03-01 that LIVISI would end its services on 2024-03-01, citing failure to make privacy, independence and sustainability profitable (an earlier note on digitalzimmer gave 2024-02-01; the final date was 2024-03-01). Local SmartHome became available for all controllers on 2022-09-26. The vendor's 2022-09-30 post said Local SmartHome still partly needed internet and the cloud then; what still needs internet after 2024-03-01 is not stated by any source read. digitalzimmer reported the shutdown on 2024-03-01. The vendor community went read-only, and its content lives on at lsh.community, a privately run site that says it is not LIVISI's legal successor. Company status: LIVISI GmbH was registered 2018-12-11 at Amtsgericht Essen (HRB 29622), c/o innogy SE, Dortmund. A register aggregator shows that entry deleted and a later Livisi GmbH record in Munich, which reads as a seat move, but this was not confirmed against the official register. No source found for an insolvency or liquidation. The vendor domains (livisi.de, community.livisi.de, developer.services-smarthome.de) did not resolve on 2026-10-25.
cloud.vendor_service: LIVISI SmartHome services (ex innogy SmartHome / RWE SmartHome cloud)

get_capabilities.description: List every capability (the controllable or readable function of a device) with its type, owning device link and config.
get_capabilities.notes: A JSON ARRAY (payload_formats.CapabilityList). Join to devices on capability.device == "/device/" + device.id.

get_capability_state.description: One capability's current state: a map of property name to {value, lastChanged}.

capability_id.description: 32 lower-case hex characters: the id of a capability from get_capabilities (the part after /capability/).

get_capability_states.description: Every capability's current state in one request.
get_capability_states.notes: A JSON ARRAY of {id, state} objects (openHAB reads it as such). Each state is a CapabilityState property map.

get_device_state.description: One device's state (for the controller: CPU, memory, disk, reboot time, configVersion).
get_device_state.notes: SHC 1 wraps the property map in {"state": {...}}; SHC 2 returns the map itself (openHAB and planbnet both branch on this).

device_id.description: 32 lower-case hex characters: a device id from get_devices.

get_devices.description: List every device the controller knows, including the controller itself and virtual devices.
get_devices.notes: A JSON ARRAY (payload_formats.DeviceList). The controller's own entry has type SHC (SHC 1) or SHCA (SHC 2).

get_locations.description: Rooms: id plus config.name. Devices link to them as /location/<id>.

get_messages.description: Controller messages: low battery, device unreachable, update available, update completed.
get_messages.notes: A JSON ARRAY (payload_formats.MessageList). The only place battery-low and unreachable flags come from when polling.

get_status.description: Controller identity and configuration version: which generation, which firmware, whether the config changed.
get_status.notes: Shape differs by generation (payload_formats.StatusReply): SHC 1 answers a flat object, SHC 2 nests the gateway facts under "gateway". The planbnet library reads controllerType at the top level on both and branches on "Classic" vs "Avatar". configVersion changes whenever the configuration changes (devices added, renamed, rules edited). openHAB polls it to know when to re-read the device list.

get_token.description: Log in. OAuth2 resource-owner password grant against the controller itself: fixed user "admin", the local password, fixed client credentials in HTTP Basic. The reply's access_token is the bearer token for everything else.
get_token.example_notes: Rendered with an invented password "Example-Pass1!". The planbnet library sends exactly this JSON body. openHAB's generic OAuth2 client sends the same three fields form-encoded (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) with the same Basic header, so the controller accepts both encodings as far as the two clients show. JSON is the form documented here.
get_token.notes: Failure modes seen by the planbnet library: a JSON reply without access_token and with errorcode 2003 (invalid client credentials) or 2009 (invalid user credentials) means a wrong password. HTTP 401 means the same. A refused TCP connection means a wrong address or a controller that is not on the network.

password.description: The Local SmartHome password the owner set in the controller's local web app. It is not the label serial or PIN, which is only the first login default. JSON-escape it when it is substituted, because a special character is mandatory and may be a quote or backslash.

returns.description: JWT bearer token. The only field both reference clients read.
returns.name: access_token

restart_controller.advanced_reason: Reboots the SmartHome controller. Every device it controls stops responding to the app and to rules until it is back, typically for a few minutes. Nothing is erased; if it does not return, power-cycle it.
restart_controller.description: Reboot the controller (Restart action addressed to the controller DEVICE, not a capability).
restart_controller.example_notes: Rendered with an invented controller id.
restart_controller.notes: openHAB sends a free-text "reason" param; the planbnet library sends empty params, so the reason is optional. The controller reboots immediately and usually drops the connection without answering, so treat a server disconnect on this request as success.

device_id.description: Id of the controller's own entry in get_devices (type SHC or SHCA).

set_dim_level.description: Set a DimmerActuator capability's level (plug dimmer PSD, in-wall dimmer ISD2). 0 is off.

capability_id.description: Id of the device's DimmerActuator capability.

dim_level.description: Brightness in percent, sent as a JSON integer. The planbnet integration turns a light off by writing 0 and fully on by writing 100.

set_operation_mode.description: Switch a ThermostatActuator between the controller's schedule (Auto) and manual (Manu). Setting one thermostat of a room is enough; the controller syncs the rest (planbnet note).

capability_id.description: Id of a ThermostatActuator capability (a RoomSetpoint config's underlyingCapabilityIds lists them, comma-separated).

operation_mode.description: "Auto" follows the controller's heating schedule; "Manu" holds the manual setpoint. Spelled exactly so (Manu, not Manual).

set_room_setpoint.description: Set a room's target temperature on the RoomSetpoint capability of the room's virtual heating device (VRCC), on an SHC 2. This is the planbnet integration's route. The controller propagates it to the room's thermostats.
set_room_setpoint.example_notes: Rendered with setpoint_temperature=20. SHC 2 only; set_room_setpoint_classic is the SHC 1 spelling.

capability_id.description: Id of the VRCC device's RoomSetpoint capability.

setpoint_temperature.description: Target in degrees Celsius. Clamp to the capability config's minTemperature/maxTemperature when present.

set_room_setpoint_classic.description: As set_room_setpoint, on an SHC 1, where the same RoomSetpoint property is spelled pointTemperature.

capability_id.description: Id of the VRCC device's RoomSetpoint capability.

set_shutter_level.description: Move a RollerShutterActuator (in-wall shutter ISR2) to a position.
set_shutter_level.notes: The two references disagree on the namespace of this one SetState: the planbnet integration sends CosipDevices.RWE, openHAB sends the default core.RWE. Both are in production use. CosipDevices.RWE is documented here because the ramp commands below use it in both clients. If the controller answers an errorcode, retry with core.RWE.

capability_id.description: Id of the device's RollerShutterActuator capability.

shutter_level.description: Position in percent. openHAB treats 100 as fully up (open) and 0 as fully down; it offers an `invert` option because installations differ.

set_thermostat_point_temperature.description: Set the target temperature on a ThermostatActuator capability (radiator thermostats RST/RST2, wall thermostat WRT). This is openHAB's route, used unchanged on both controller generations.

capability_id.description: Id of the thermostat device's ThermostatActuator capability.

point_temperature.description: Target temperature in degrees Celsius, as a JSON number. 6-30 is the range openHAB and the planbnet integration use; the RoomSetpoint capability's config may carry tighter minTemperature/maxTemperature.

set_variable.description: Set a virtual boolean variable (device type VariableActuator, capability type BooleanStateActuator) used in the controller's own rules.

capability_id.description: Id of the VariableActuator device's BooleanStateActuator capability.

value.description: New state of the variable, as a JSON boolean.

shutter_down.description: Start moving a shutter down (StartRamp RampDown).

shutter_stop.description: Stop a moving shutter (StopRamp, no params).

shutter_up.description: Start moving a shutter up (StartRamp RampUp).

switch_on.description: Turn a SwitchActuator capability on (plugs PSS/PSSO/BT-PSS, in-wall switch ISS2).
switch_on.example_notes: Rendered with an invented capability id. Reply: payload_formats.ActionReply.

capability_id.description: Id of the device's SwitchActuator capability (type "SwitchActuator" in get_capabilities).

identification.notes: No scan signal is documented: no mDNS service type, no SSDP target, no vetted MAC prefix. One openHAB test fixture shows an SHC 1 with a MAC in eQ-3's 00:1a:22 block, which fits eQ-3 having built hardware for RWE, but a single fixture is not enough to declare a prefix. Identify the controller after the user enters its address: GET /status (with a token) and read controllerType.

device.manufacturer: LIVISI GmbH (formerly innogy SmartHome / RWE SmartHome)
device.name: LIVISI SmartHome Controller (SHC 1 / SHC 2), Local SmartHome API
device.notes:
The LIVISI SmartHome Controller (SHC) is a hub for LIVISI's own 868 MHz radio devices (plugs, in-wall switches/dimmers/shutter actuators, radiator and wall thermostats, window/door contacts, motion and smoke detectors, remotes, sirens) sold since the RWE SmartHome and innogy SmartHome days. Two hardware generations exist: SHC 1 (LIVISI calls it "Classic"; device type "SHC") and SHC 2 ("2nd generation", device type "SHCA", controllerType "Avatar" in the status reply).
LIVISI announced on 2022-03-01 that its SmartHome services would end on 2024-03-01, and switched them off that day. "Local SmartHome" — a local web app plus a local copy of the cloud API on the controller — has been available for every controller since 2022-09-26 and was activated automatically by the January/February 2024 controller updates. It is now the only control path. The child devices are proprietary LIVISI radio (not Zigbee or Z-Wave), so unlike the devolo case they cannot be moved to a third-party controller: keeping the SHC alive is the rescue.
The local link is unencrypted HTTP. The bearer token and the local password cross the LAN in clear, and the WebSocket carries the token in its query string. Keep the controller on a trusted or isolated network; never port-forward it.
Host names: the vendor how-to says the local web app answers at http://SMARTHOME01 (SHC 1) or http://SHCONTROLLER01 (SHC 2), with a higher number when several controllers share a LAN, and recommends a fixed IP because the name does not always resolve. The control API is on port 8080 on both generations.

openness.notes: LIVISI published developer documentation for its cloud API ("CAPI", developer.services-smarthome.de) and described the Local SmartHome API as a copy of that API served by the controller, authenticated with the OAuth2 resource-owner password grant and the fixed user "admin". The vendor site is gone (the domains no longer resolve as of 2026-10-25), so the documentation survives only in the Wayback Machine. The SHC 1 / SHC 2 differences (event port, status shape, setpoint property name, device-state wrapper) were never in that documentation; they are taken from the openHAB binding and the planbnet/livisi library, which is why `reverse_engineered` is true.

upstream_docs.covers: The errorcode table in payload_formats.ErrorReply. The live developer site no longer resolves.
upstream_docs.title: LIVISI SmartHome developer documentation, error codes (Wayback snapshot 2023-03-21)

issued_to_client: OAuth2 access_token (a JWT bearer token), from POST /auth/token. It expires; re-request with the stored password.
credentials.notes: This spec documents Ethernet bring-up only, so no Wi-Fi passphrase crosses any link here. The SHC 2 status reply reports Wi-Fi hotspot and WPS state, so it has a radio, but its Wi-Fi onboarding is not documented by any source read. The local password and the token both travel in clear HTTP.
stored_on_device: Local SmartHome password for the fixed user admin
Radio pairing keys for the LIVISI devices taught to the controller (not exposed by the API)

factory_reset.description: The successor community lists "factory reset" among states in which the local web app is unavailable, so the controller has one, but nothing read here describes the buttons or timing. A lost local password is the case most owners will hit, and its recovery is equally undocumented here. Do not guess: without the cloud, a reset controller's devices have to be re-taught locally, and how far that works offline is unknown.
factory_reset.effect: Not established from public sources. A reset would presumably clear the device pairings and rules and the local password, but no source read for this spec gives a procedure or says what survives.

methods.description: Wire the controller to the LAN and make sure its firmware is at least the Local SmartHome release (variants). Open the local web app at http://<controller>/, log in with the default from the label, set the local password, and accept the terms. A client then POSTs /auth/token on port 8080 as user "admin" with that password and uses the returned access_token as a bearer token on every request and as the token query parameter of the event WebSocket.

access_token.notes: A JWT. Send it as "Authorization: Bearer <token>" on every API request and as ?token=<url-encoded token> on the event WebSocket. It expires: the planbnet library reads the JWT exp claim and also treats errorcode 2007 as expiry. In either case, run get_token again with the stored local_password and retry once. The lifetime is not documented.

local_password.notes: The local password the owner set in the Local SmartHome web app. It is not the label default, which the web app forces the owner to change. The user name is always "admin": Local SmartHome is a single-user system. Rules from the vendor FAQ: at least 10 characters with upper case, lower case, a digit and a special character, and no "?". Store it, because a token is re-requested with it whenever the old one expires.

methods.name: Ethernet, Local SmartHome web app, then token login

steps.action: Connect the controller to the router with Ethernet and power it; reserve its DHCP address in the router.
steps.expect: The controller takes a DHCP lease; its local web app answers on http://<address>/.

steps.action: Check the controller firmware meets the Local SmartHome minimum for its generation (SHC 1: 1.914-3.1.1043.0; SHC 2: 8.17-1.2.39.443).
steps.notes: Controllers updated in January/February 2024 had Local SmartHome activated automatically; unregistered controllers run it from the start.

steps.action: Open http://<address>/ in a browser and log in with the label default: SHC 1 uses the digits after 'SN' on the underside label (no spaces); SHC 2 uses the characters after 'PIN:' on the same label.
steps.expect: The web app asks for a new password and for the terms to be accepted.

steps.action: On SHC 1 with controller software 3.1.1056.0 or later, press the button on the controller when the web app asks for physical confirmation.
steps.notes: Vendor post edited 2022-11-07. Which button is not named in the sources; the vendor FAQ does not state this step for SHC 2.

steps.action: Set the new local password (at least 10 characters, A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and a special character, no '?') and accept the terms.
Request a token: POST /auth/token on port 8080 with HTTP Basic clientId:clientPass and the JSON body {username: admin, password: <local password>, grant_type: password}.
steps.expect: 200 with a JSON object carrying access_token. Wrong password: errorcode 2009 (or 2003), or HTTP 401.

arguments.description: The local password set in the web app.
arguments.name: password

cloud.local_alternative: Local SmartHome, the primary method above: local web app plus the port-8080 API. It needs no account.
cloud.provider: LIVISI SmartHome services (ex innogy SmartHome / RWE SmartHome)

methods.description: The original route: the controller was registered to a LIVISI account and managed through the vendor app and cloud, which also had an in-app switch (Settings > General settings > Local SmartHome > Activate). The services and accounts were shut down on 2024-03-01 and their data deleted. Documented for completeness only.
methods.name: LIVISI app and cloud account (retired 2024-03-01)

steps.action: In the LIVISI app, open Settings > General settings > Local SmartHome and tap Activate.

setup.notes: A controller comes up on Ethernet by DHCP. Local SmartHome must then be initialised once in the controller's local web app: log in with the label default, set a new local password and accept the terms. Every API client then logs in as the fixed user "admin" with that password and gets a bearer token. Firmware minimums and the default-password rules come from LIVISI's official community post of 2022-09-30. The password rules come from the LIVISI FAQ as preserved by the successor community. None of it has been run by this project.

rejoin.notes: Inferred, not sourced: the controller is a wired DHCP client, so a new router means a new lease and nothing else. The local password and device pairings live on the controller. The vendor FAQ's advice to fix the IP exists because clients are configured with an address, not a discovered identity. Update the client's host after a move.

variants.notes: Device type "SHC" in GET /device. Local SmartHome needs firmware 1.914-3.1.1043.0 or later (first update to 1.913-3.0.1008.0). WebSocket events on port 8080. GET /status carries serialNumber, osVersion, appVersion and configVersion at the top level. GET /device/{id}/state wraps the property map in a "state" object. Controller load properties are spelled CPULoad, memoryLoad and OSState. Room setpoints are written as pointTemperature. From controller software 3.1.1056.0, first-time Local SmartHome setup has to be confirmed with a button press on the controller. The firmware string is osVersion-appVersion (the openHAB fixture's 1.914 and 3.1.1025.0 have that form).

Device type "SHCA" in GET /device. Local SmartHome needs firmware 8.17-1.2.39.443 or later (first update to 8.17-1.1.36.426); openHAB states the minimum as 1.2.x. WebSocket events on port 9090. GET /status nests serialNumber, osVersion, appVersion, configVersion, operationStatus and network details under a "gateway" object. GET /device/{id}/state returns the property map unwrapped. Controller load properties are spelled cpuUsage, memoryUsage and operationStatus. Room setpoints are written as setpointTemperature. The planbnet library opens up to 10 concurrent HTTP connections to an SHC 2 against 1 to an SHC 1.

http_endpoints.description: OAuth2 password grant (commands.get_token). Client auth: HTTP Basic clientId:clientPass. Port 8080, plain HTTP. On success the planbnet library reads access_token only. openHAB parses a standard OAuth2 token response, which suggests token_type and expires_in are there too, but the field list beyond access_token is unverified.

http_endpoints.description: The single write endpoint: every control is an action object naming a type (SetState, StartRamp, StopRamp, Restart), a namespace, a target link (/capability/<id> or /device/<id>) and params, each param wrapped as {"type": "Constant", "value": ...} (payload_formats.ActionRequest). The reply is payload_formats.ActionReply. The planbnet library also sends an "id" field with a random 32-hex value; openHAB does not, so it is optional.

covers: Reading every device and capability state, and push updates
Switching, dimming, shutter position and ramps, thermostat setpoints and Auto/Manu mode, virtual variables, siren channel
not_covered: Teaching new radio devices to the controller and editing rules: done in the local web app, not through any API documented here
Remote access: there is none; use a VPN into the LAN, never a port forward
Factory reset and lost-password recovery: undocumented
local_access.summary: Local SmartHome on the controller: HTTP API on 8080 with a password-grant bearer token, WebSocket events on 9090 (SHC 2) or 8080 (SHC 1). It needs no account and survived the cloud shutdown. openHAB, Home Assistant (core `livisi` integration, and the planbnet/livisi_unofficial custom integration) and ioBroker speak it.

ErrorReply.description: How the controller reports a failed request: a JSON object with an integer errorcode, carried in place of the normal reply. Check every reply object for errorcode before reading it.
ErrorReply.example: {"errorcode":2007,"description":"The lifetime of the token has expired.","messages":[]}

fields.description: Integer error code; table in `values`.
fields.name: errorcode

fields.description: Human-readable text.
fields.name: description

fields.description: Optional array of further strings.
fields.name: messages

parse_rules: Parse the body as JSON. An object with an `errorcode` key is an error, whatever the HTTP status.
2007 means the token expired: run get_token with the stored password and resend the original request once. A second error after that is real.
2003 and 2009 on get_token mean wrong credentials: ask the owner for the local password again; do not retry in a loop (2013 is an account lock).
Other codes are terminal for that request; surface `description`.

values.2006: A connection already exists for this session.
values.2007: Token lifetime expired: get a new token and retry once.
values.2008: Login attempted from a different client provider.
values.3001: Request content invalid, cannot be parsed.
values.3005: Too many entities of this type.
values.4002: Permission to trigger action not allowed.
values.5001: Could not obtain exclusive access to the configuration.

remaining_unknowns: Per-device entities are not declared. GET /device, /capability and /capability/states answer JSON arrays, and the schema's `instances` needs an object keyed by child id, so a spec-driven client cannot enumerate switches, dimmers or thermostats from this file. The commands are complete; binding them needs array-keyed instances (`instances.keyed_by` over an array element field) or a join of capability -> device.
Token reply fields beyond access_token (token_type, expires_in, refresh_token) and the token lifetime are not stated by either reference client; the example's extra fields are illustrative.

Whether /status carries controllerType at the top level on SHC 2 alongside the `gateway` object: the planbnet library reads it there, while openHAB's SHC 2 fixture shows only `gateway`. The GET /device controller type (SHC vs SHCA) is the safe fallback discriminator.
Namespace for shutterLevel SetState: CosipDevices.RWE (planbnet) vs core.RWE (openHAB).
Which button confirms first-time Local SmartHome setup on SHC 1 from software 3.1.1056.0, and whether SHC 2 has an equivalent step.
Factory reset procedure and local password recovery for either generation.
Whether anything in Local SmartHome still needs internet after the 2024-03-01 shutdown (the 2022-09-30 vendor post said it partly did at the time).
No mDNS/SSDP announcement is documented; only the host names SMARTHOME01 / SHCONTROLLER01 from the vendor how-to. A LAN capture would settle discovery.
LIVISI GmbH's corporate status after the shutdown: the Essen register entry shows deleted, apparently a move to Munich; no insolvency or liquidation source found.
Whether firmware updates are still obtainable after the shutdown (the successor community has an 'Updating the SHC' guide; not read).

channels.description: Server push only. Each text frame is one JSON event (payload_formats.Event): StateChanged with a flat properties map for a /capability/<id> or /device/<id> source, ButtonPressed and MotionDetected for button and motion capabilities, MessageCreated / MessageDeleted / NewMessageReceived for the message list, ConfigurationChanged when configVersion moves, plus Disconnect.
channels.name: events

websocket.notes: Pick the port by generation rather than by trial: 9090 on SHC 2, 8080 on SHC 1 (variants; both reference clients branch on the controller type). The fallback entry is the SHC 1 address. The token is the same access_token as the HTTP API, URL-encoded into the query string. openHAB encodes it on both generations; the planbnet library only on SHC 2, and a JWT is URL-safe apart from padding anyway. There is no other handshake and nothing is sent by the client. openHAB reconnects when no frame arrives for 900 s (its default idle timeout), and the planbnet library pings every 10 s with a 10 s timeout. On token expiry, get a new token and reconnect. openHAB polls the controller's own CPU/memory state on SHC 1 every minute because, per its source, the SHC 1 does not push those events; SHC 2 does.
